raw_text:
- This research aims to investigate and explain the variations in completion times between sites employing the same nominal work process. The scope is confined to examining measurable factors contributing to these differences and distinguishing between competing explanations.

Assumptions
- The completion times are consistent and meaningful measures of productivity.
- Differences in completion times can be attributed to factors within the examined scope.

Research design
- We will utilize a mixed-methods design, combining both qualitative (case studies, interviews) and quantitative (surveys, time-tracking software) analyses to paint a comprehensive picture of site performance.

Data or evidence needed
- Surveys to collect quantitative data on site-specific variables (e.g., resource allocation, employee skills).
- Time-tracking logs to provide objective completion-time data.
- Case study interviews with employees and managers to gather qualitative insights into perceived work processes.

Measurement
- Quantitative variables: completion time, resources per task, employee productivity.
- Qualitative variables: process deviations, employee suggestions, managerial decisions.

Analysis
- Quantitative analysis: Descriptive statistics to summarize data, regression analysis to identify significant predictors of completion time.
- Qualitative analysis: Thematic analysis of interviews to define patterns and themes related to process efficacy.

Decision / stopping rule
- The research will conclude if quantitative analysis reveals significant predictors of completion time across sites and qualitative evidence supports or contradicts those findings.

Limitations
- Possible selection bias in survey responses.
- Self-reported data on time and productivity may not be entirely accurate.
- Limited sample size, especially for qualitative data, might restrict generalizability.
- Rapid changes in work processes or external factors influencing outcomes could occur during the study period, affecting findings.
